Fix a selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ as in
[[def-kl-projection-set-and-relative-kl-neighborhoods]]. Since its KL value is
finite, $p_{\theta^*}>0$ $P_0$-almost surely. For each $\theta\in\Theta$,
define the nonnegative set function
$$Q_\theta(A):=\int_A\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)}\,P_0(dx), \qquad A\in\mathcal A,$$
where the ratio is assigned value $0$ on the $P_0$-null set
$\{p_{\theta^*}=0\}$. Write
$$q_\theta:=Q_\theta(\mathsf X) =\mathbb E_{P_0}\left[\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}\right]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $q_\theta\ne1$, $Q_\theta$ is not a probability law. The local
sigma-finiteness lemma proves that it is a measure. The local product-measure
lemma then constructs $Q_\theta^n$ and proves its density relative to $P_0^n$
is $\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(X_i)/p_{\theta^*}(X_i)$.

For a measurable test $\phi_n:\mathsf X^n\to[0,1]$,
Once that product measure has been constructed,
$Q_\theta^n(1-\phi_n)$ means the nonnegative integral of $1-\phi_n$ under it.
It may be infinite; a hypothesis that this quantity tends to zero in
particular requires it to be finite for all sufficiently large $n$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta$ and define $r_\theta=p_\theta/p_{\theta^*}$ on $\{p_{\theta^*}>0\}$ and $r_\theta=0$ elsewhere. By [F1] and [F2], $r_\theta$ is nonnegative, measurable, and finite $P_0$-almost surely. Thus $Q_\theta(A)=\int_A r_\theta\,dP_0$ is defined for every $A\in\mathcal A$.

By [F3], $Q_\theta$ is a measure. For each integer $k\ge1$, set $E_k=\{x:r_\theta(x)\le k\}$. The ratio convention in [F1] and the finite-valued density hypothesis make $r_\theta$ finite everywhere, so the $E_k$ increase to $\mathsf X$. Moreover, $Q_\theta(E_k)=\int_{E_k}r_\theta\,dP_0\le kP_0(E_k)\le k$ by [F4]. Thus $(E_k)_{k\ge1}$ is a countable cover by finite-$Q_\theta$-measure sets, and $Q_\theta$ is sigma-finite.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 1.1: Q_theta(empty)=integral_empty r_theta dP0=0. An empty sample space itself cannot carry the stipulated probability P0.
Step 1.1 uses ratio zero on {p_theta*=0}; zeros of p_theta on its positive denominator support give r_theta=0 and cause neither division by zero nor infinite density.
Statement: Q_theta* has total mass one. Step 2.1 already starts the exhaustion at k=1, with Q_theta(E_1)<=1.
Steps 1.1–2.1 also apply when P0 is a point mass: the finite ratio at its supporting point yields a finite tilt and the same countable exhaustion.
Step 2.1 bounds Q_theta(E_k)<=k although Q_theta(X) may be infinite; sigma-finiteness needs these finite pieces rather than finite total mass.
Step 2.1 explicitly defines E_k={r_theta<=k} for each integer k>=1; no choice of an unspecified exhaustion is needed.

boundaries.reason: Statement proves sigma-finiteness from the supplied finite density ratio; it does not characterize every sigma-finite measure as a likelihood tilt.
Statement separately records unit mass at theta*; sigma-finiteness alone is not asserted to imply theta is a minimizer or q_theta=1.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC as required by the imported directional KL convention
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\rho)$ be a
metric space, where $\mathcal T$ is its Borel sigma-algebra. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sample space with a fixed sigma-finite
dominating measure. Suppose the supplied finite-valued densities
$(\theta,x)\mapsto p_\theta(x)$ and $x\mapsto p_0(x)$ are jointly measurable
and normalized relative to $\mu$, and observations are IID from $P_0$. Use
the directional convention for [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]:
$$K(\theta):=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta).$$
Assume $K^*:=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}K(\theta)<\infty$ and
$$\Theta^*:=\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta)=K^*\}\ne\varnothing.$$
The set $\Theta^*$ is the **KL projection set** of the truth onto the model.
The **distance to the KL projection set** is
$$d(\theta,\Theta^*):=\inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta^*}\rho(\theta,\vartheta).$$
A **relative KL neighborhood** of $\Theta^*$ of radius $\epsilon>0$ is
$$B_\epsilon:=\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta)-K^*\le\epsilon\}.$$

For any selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ with finite contrast, the relative
contrast on $B_\epsilon$ satisfies
$$K(\theta)-K^*=-\mathbb E_{P_0}\log\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}$$
whenever the displayed log ratio is integrable. This definition allows
$\Theta^*$ to contain multiple parameters and does not assert that the
posterior selects one of them.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

derivations.claim: The jointly measurable finite-valued densities and [F12], [F13] make $\{(\theta,x):p_\theta(x)=0\}$ measurable. The density formula gives $P_0\ll P_\theta$ exactly when $\int 1_{\{p_\theta=0\}}p_0\,d\mu=0$; Tonelli [F4] makes this condition measurable in $\theta$. On this measurable set, the extended log-density parts defining $K(\theta)$ are product-measurable and Tonelli makes their section integrals measurable; outside it the KL value is $+\infty$ by [F2]. Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta)$ and $B_\epsilon$ are measurable. By [F1], for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$, $\mathbb E_{P_0}\log\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)} =-\bigl(K(\theta)-K^*\bigr)\ge-\epsilon.$ Both KL values are finite on this set, so [F2] makes the log ratio integrable.

For each fixed $\theta$ in this full-prior subset of $B_\epsilon$, $L_i^\theta:=\log(p_\theta(X_i)/p_{\theta^*}(X_i))$ are IID integrable real variables: the data are IID and [F6] preserves independence under the measurable log-ratio map. By [F5], $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n L_i^\theta \longrightarrow-\bigl(K(\theta)-K^*\bigr)\ge-\epsilon \quad P_0^\infty\text{-almost surely}.$ The event of this convergence is jointly measurable in $(\theta,X_1,X_2,\ldots)$. Tonelli [F4] applied to the indicator of its failure, under $\Pi|_{B_\epsilon}\times P_0^\infty$, therefore gives a $P_0^\infty$-full event on which convergence holds for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$.

For fixed $n$, the finite product measures $\mu^n$ and $P_0^n$ exist by [F17]. The nonnegative jointly measurable likelihood $\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i)$ is product-measurable by [F15] and integrates to one over $\mu^n$ for every $\theta$, by [F16] and repeated integration. Tonelli [F4] therefore gives $\int_{\mathsf X^n}\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i)\, \Pi(d\theta)\,\mu^n(dx_{1:n})=1.$ Let $Z_n(x_{1:n})=\int_\Theta\prod_i p_\theta(x_i)\Pi(d\theta)$. By [F11], $Z_n<\infty$ $\mu^n$-almost everywhere. The sample vector has law $P_0^n$ by [F9]. Its product density relative to $\mu^n$ is $\prod_i p_0(x_i)$: repeated Tonelli gives this density's rectangle formula, and [F10] identifies the resulting measure with $P_0^n$. Therefore $Z_n<\infty$ $P_0^n$-almost surely.

For $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$, finite KL gives $P_0\ll P_\theta$ by [F2], so $p_\theta(X_i)>0$ almost surely for each coordinate. The coordinate products are measurable by [F15]; Tonelli [F4] applied to the indicator of a zero likelihood shows that, for $P_0^n$-almost every sample, $p_\theta(X_i)>0$ for every $i$ for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$. Since $\Pi(B_\epsilon)>0$, $Z_n>0$. Finally, $p_{\theta^*}(X_i)$ is finite and positive $P_0$-almost surely, so the relative denominator $D_n$ is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely.

Fix $\alpha>\epsilon$ and choose $\alpha'$ with $\epsilon<\alpha'<\alpha$. On the event from step 1.2, for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$ the log likelihood average is eventually greater than $-\alpha'$. Therefore $e^{n\alpha}\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_{\theta^*}(X_i)} \ge e^{n(\alpha-\alpha')}\longrightarrow+\infty.$ Fatou's lemma [F14] for the nonnegative integrands gives $\liminf_{n\to\infty}e^{n\alpha}D_n \ge\int_{B_\epsilon}\liminf_{n\to\infty} e^{n\alpha}\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_{\theta^*}(X_i)} \,\Pi(d\theta)=+\infty,$ since $\Pi(B_\epsilon)>0$. Hence $D_n\ge e^{-n\alpha}$ eventually.
Steps 1.3–2.2 establish finite-positive evidence, and step 2.2 establishes the eventual exponential lower bound asserted in the Statement.

$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta$ and $n\ge1$. By [F2] and [F3], the product measures $Q_\theta^n$ and $P_0^n$ exist and are sigma-finite. For $x_{1:n}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, every coordinate map is measurable by [F7], so $f_n(x_{1:n}):=\prod_{i=1}^n r_\theta(x_i)$ is nonnegative and measurable.

Define $R_n(A):=\int_A f_n\,dP_0^n$ on the product sigma-algebra. By [F6], $R_n$ is a measure. For every measurable rectangle $A_1\times\cdots\times A_n$, repeated Tonelli integration [F5] gives $R_n(A_1\times\cdots\times A_n) =\prod_{i=1}^n\int_{A_i}r_\theta\,dP_0 =\prod_{i=1}^n Q_\theta(A_i) =Q_\theta^n(A_1\times\cdots\times A_n),$ where the final equality is [F4]'s rectangle formula.

The measures $R_n$ and $Q_\theta^n$ agree on the generating pi-system of measurable rectangles by step 2.1. The product-measure theorem [F4] gives uniqueness for this rectangle formula, so $R_n=Q_\theta^n$ on the whole product sigma-algebra. By the definition of $R_n$, its density is $f_n=\prod_{i=1}^n r_\theta(x_i)$, as claimed.

boundaries.reason: Statement explicitly quantifies over integers n>=1; the detected product is over this nonempty coordinate set, and no zeroth product-measure construction is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 defines finite nonnegative coordinate ratios using the zero-denominator convention. If any factor is zero the product density is zero; no quotient by that product occurs.
Statement at n=1 reduces to Q_theta=r_theta P0, and step 2.1 gives R_1(A_1)=integral_A1 r_theta dP0=Q_theta(A_1).
Steps 1.1–3.1 allow Q_theta=P0; then r_theta=1 P0-almost surely and the product density is one P0^n-almost surely.
Step 2.1 uses nonnegative Tonelli even if a rectangle has infinite Q_theta measure; sigma-finite factors suffice and no normalization to probability is asserted.
Step 1.1 fixes theta and a positive integer n, and step 2.1 defines R_n explicitly; the cited sigma-finite product theorem supplies the unique product rather than selecting versions.

boundaries.reason: Statement derives the density of the already defined product likelihood tilt; it does not assert a characterization of arbitrary measures from a candidate density.
Statement constructs Q_theta^n for n>=1 from Q_theta and proves its product density; it makes no inference recovering a KL minimizer from a product measure.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC as required by the imported directional KL convention
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\rho)$ be a
metric space, where $\mathcal T$ is its Borel sigma-algebra. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sample space with a fixed sigma-finite
dominating measure. Suppose the supplied finite-valued densities
$(\theta,x)\mapsto p_\theta(x)$ and $x\mapsto p_0(x)$ are jointly measurable
and normalized relative to $\mu$, and observations are IID from $P_0$. Use
the directional convention for [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]:
$$K(\theta):=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta).$$
Assume $K^*:=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}K(\theta)<\infty$ and
$$\Theta^*:=\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta)=K^*\}\ne\varnothing.$$
The set $\Theta^*$ is the **KL projection set** of the truth onto the model.
The **distance to the KL projection set** is
$$d(\theta,\Theta^*):=\inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta^*}\rho(\theta,\vartheta).$$
A **relative KL neighborhood** of $\Theta^*$ of radius $\epsilon>0$ is
$$B_\epsilon:=\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta)-K^*\le\epsilon\}.$$

For any selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ with finite contrast, the relative
contrast on $B_\epsilon$ satisfies
$$K(\theta)-K^*=-\mathbb E_{P_0}\log\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}$$
whenever the displayed log ratio is integrable. This definition allows
$\Theta^*$ to contain multiple parameters and does not assert that the
posterior selects one of them.

Fix a selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ as in
[[def-kl-projection-set-and-relative-kl-neighborhoods]]. Since its KL value is
finite, $p_{\theta^*}>0$ $P_0$-almost surely. For each $\theta\in\Theta$,
define the nonnegative set function
$$Q_\theta(A):=\int_A\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)}\,P_0(dx), \qquad A\in\mathcal A,$$
where the ratio is assigned value $0$ on the $P_0$-null set
$\{p_{\theta^*}=0\}$. Write
$$q_\theta:=Q_\theta(\mathsf X) =\mathbb E_{P_0}\left[\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}\right]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $q_\theta\ne1$, $Q_\theta$ is not a probability law. The local
sigma-finiteness lemma proves that it is a measure. The local product-measure
lemma then constructs $Q_\theta^n$ and proves its density relative to $P_0^n$
is $\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(X_i)/p_{\theta^*}(X_i)$.

For a measurable test $\phi_n:\mathsf X^n\to[0,1]$,
Once that product measure has been constructed,
$Q_\theta^n(1-\phi_n)$ means the nonnegative integral of $1-\phi_n$ under it.
It may be infinite; a hypothesis that this quantity tends to zero in
particular requires it to be finite for all sufficiently large $n$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

Under the setup of [[def-likelihood-tilted-measure-at-kl-projection]] and
[[lem-likelihood-tilted-measure-is-sigma-finite]], for each $\theta$ and
integer $n\ge1$, the sigma-finite product measure $Q_\theta^n$ exists and
has density
$$\prod_{i=1}^n r_\theta(x_i),\qquad r_\theta(x):=\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)},$$
relative to $P_0^n$. Ratios are zero where $p_{\theta^*}=0$, as in the
likelihood-tilt definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta_1\ne\theta^*$ and put $r_1=p_{\theta_1}/p_{\theta^*}$ on $\{p_{\theta^*}>0\}$, with value zero on its $P_0$-null complement. The finite likelihood-ratio mean makes $r_1$ integrable. For $r_1\ge1$, [F11] gives $0\le\log r_1=\int_1^{r_1}u^{-1}du\le r_1-1\le r_1$, so the positive part is integrable. The log ratio is measurable by [F14]. Also $\mathbb E_{P_0}\log r_1 =-\bigl(K(\theta_1)-K^*\bigr)<0,$ by the extended relative-contrast hypothesis, with value $-\infty$ allowed.

For $t\downarrow0$, let $A(t)=\mathbb E_{P_0}r_1^t$. Since $r_1^t\le1+r_1$ for $0<t\le1$, [F8] gives $A(t)\to P_0(r_1>0)\le1$. If this limit is less than one, then $A(t)<1$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. If the limit equals one, split into $\{r_1\ge1\}$ and $\{0<r_1<1\}$. On the first set, $(r_1^t-1)/t\to\log r_1$ and, for fixed $t_0<1$ and $0<t\le t_0$, the mean-value theorem bounds this quotient above by $r_1^{t_0}\log r_1\le C r_1$ for a finite constant $C$: the function $r^{t_0-1}\log r$ is continuous on $[1,\infty)$ and tends to zero at infinity. On the second set, write $y=-\log r_1>0$. Then $(1-r_1^t)/t=y(1-e^{-yt})/(yt)$. The function $u\mapsto(1-e^{-u})/u$ decreases on $u>0$, since its derivative is $((u+1)e^{-u}-1)/u^2\le0$ by $e^u\ge1+u$: for $u\ge0$, $h(u)=\exp(u)-1-u$ has $h(0)=0$ by the exponential definition and $h'(u)=\exp(u)-1\ge0$ by the derivative formula and exponential monotonicity, the mean value theorem then gives $h(u)\ge0$. Hence the quotient increases to $y$ as $t\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence on the first set and monotone convergence [F9] on the second show $\frac{A(t)-1}{t}\longrightarrow \mathbb E_{P_0}\log r_1<0$ in the extended sense. Thus $A(t)<1$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$.

Choose such a $t$ with $s:=1-t$ in the left-neighborhood from the fractional-moment hypothesis. Then $M_s(\theta_1,\theta_1)=A(t)<1$. By continuity at $\theta_1$, there are an open neighborhood $G_{\theta_1}$ and $0<a_{\theta_1}<1$ such that $\sup_{\theta\in G_{\theta_1}}M_s(\theta_1,\theta)\le a_{\theta_1}$.

Define $\phi_{n,\theta_1} =\mathbf 1\left\{\prod_{i=1}^n r_1(X_i)>1\right\}.$ The score and test are measurable by [F10], [F14], and [F15]. On the rejection event the product raised to $t$ exceeds one. Repeated Tonelli integration under $P_0^n$ therefore gives $P_0^n\phi_{n,\theta_1} \le \left(\mathbb E_{P_0}r_1^t\right)^n =M_s(\theta_1,\theta_1)^n \le a_{\theta_1}^n.$ For the second error, let $g_{\theta,\theta_1,s}$ be the integrand defining $M_s(\theta_1,\theta)$, with the zero and infinite conventions in the Statement. On the $P_0$-full set where $p_{\theta^*}>0$, if $p_\theta>0$ and $p_{\theta_1}>0$ then algebra gives $g_{\theta,\theta_1,s}=r_\theta r_1^{-s}$; the displayed conventions extend this identity to the boundary values. On nonrejection, $\prod_i r_1(X_i)\le1$. If every factor is positive, this gives $\prod_i r_\theta(X_i) \le\prod_i\bigl(r_\theta(X_i)r_1(X_i)^{-s}\bigr) =\prod_i g_{\theta,\theta_1,s}(X_i).$ If some $r_\theta(X_i)=0$, both the density product and the right-hand product are zero under $0\cdot\infty=0$; if some $r_1(X_i)=0$ while every $r_\theta(X_i)>0$, the right-hand product is infinite and the inequality still holds. The product-density identity [F6] and repeated Tonelli [F7] now give, for $\theta\in G_{\theta_1}$, $Q_\theta^n(1-\phi_{n,\theta_1}) \le\left(\mathbb E_{P_0}g_{\theta,\theta_1,s}(X)\right)^n =M_s(\theta_1,\theta)^n \le a_{\theta_1}^n.$ The moment hypothesis makes these integrals finite on the chosen neighborhood.

Put $C_\eta=\{\theta:\rho(\theta,\theta^*)\ge\eta\}$. If $\rho(\theta,\theta^*)<\eta$, then every $\theta'$ with $\rho(\theta',\theta)<\eta-\rho(\theta,\theta^*)$ satisfies $\rho(\theta',\theta^*)<\eta$ by [F13]. Thus the complement of $C_\eta$ is open, so $C_\eta$ is closed by [F12]. By [F5], it is compact. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in

maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.

Its normalizing integral is finite and positive, and $\mu:=E_0Y=c\int_e^\infty[y(\log y)^2]^{-1}dy=c<\infty$. For IID $Y_i$ with this density put $X_i=Y_i-\mu$ and $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. These increments are integrable, nonconstant and centered.

For $b\ge e$, direct integration gives $E_0[Y1_{\{Y>b\}}]=c/\log b$ and $P_0(Y>b)\le c/[b(\log b)^2]$. Moreover $E_0[Y^21_{\{Y\le b\}}]=c\int_e^b(\log y)^{-2}dy=O(b/(\log b)^2)$: split the integral at $\sqrt b$, bound the first part by $\sqrt b$, and the second by $4b/(\log b)^2$. Put $b_n=n/(\log n)^{3/2}$ for all sufficiently large $n$. By [F6], the probability that any of the first $n$ observations exceeds $b_n$ is $O((\log n)^{-1/2})\to0$. The variance of $\sum_{i=1}^nY_i1_{\{Y_i\le b_n\}}$ is at most $O(nb_n/(\log b_n)^2)$ by independence. Dividing this bound by $(n/\log n)^2$ gives $O(b_n/n)\to0$. Chebyshev [F4] therefore shows $S_n/(n/\log n)=-c\log n/\log b_n+o_{P_0}(1)\to-c$. Define $a_n=cn/(2\log n)$ and $\phi_n=1_{\{S_n>-a_n\}}$ for $n\ge3$, with arbitrary tests for $n<3$. It follows that $P_0^n\phi_n\to0$.

By [F3], the hitting times $T_j=\inf\{n\ge1:S_n\ge j\}$ are finite almost surely for every positive integer $j$. Define recursively $N_0=0$ and let $N_j$ be the least integer at least $\max(j,N_{j-1}+1)$ with $P_0(T_j>N_j)\le2^{-j}$. Such an integer exists since $T_j<\infty$ almost surely. Put $\epsilon_j=N_j^{-1}$. Thus $\epsilon_j>0$ and $\epsilon_j\to0$; these constants depend only on the true law, not the realized observations. By [F5], $T_j\le N_j$ eventually almost surely. Also $T_j\to\infty$ almost surely, since finitely many finite partial sums cannot exceed arbitrarily large levels.

Take sample space $\mathsf X=[e,\infty)\sqcup\{z\}$ with its disjoint-union Borel sigma-algebra and dominating measure equal to Lebesgue measure plus $\delta_z$. Set $p_0(y)=f(y)$ and $p_0(z)=0$. On the continuous part supply $p_*(y)=f(y)e^{-2y}$ and $p_j(y)=f(y)e^{-y-\mu-\epsilon_j}$; give each density its remaining mass at $z$. Both continuous masses are strictly between zero and one, so these atom masses are positive, and every density is finite and normalized. Take $\Theta=\{*\}\sqcup\mathbb N$ with the discrete metric and its Borel sigma-algebra; the supplied density family is jointly measurable. By [F1], $K(*)=2\mu<\infty$ and $K(j)=E_0(Y+\mu+\epsilon_j)=2\mu+\epsilon_j$, so $\Theta^*=\{*\}$. All relevant log ratios are integrable because $E_0Y<\infty$.

On the $P_0$-support, the tilt at $j$ has density $r_j(y)=e^{y-\mu-\epsilon_j}=e^{X-\epsilon_j}$. Its total mass is infinite, since $\int_e^\infty e^y f(y)dy=\infty$, but the finite pointwise density makes it sigma-finite by [F2]. Its product density is $e^{S_n-n\epsilon_j}$. On $\{\phi_n=0\}$ this is at most $e^{-a_n}$, uniformly in $j$, and hence $\sup_jQ_j^n(1-\phi_n)\le e^{-a_n}\to0$. For $0<\eta<1$, the set at distance greater than $\eta$ from $\Theta^*$ is precisely $\mathbb N$, so these same tests satisfy both required weak errors. For $\eta\ge1$ that set is empty and the type-II requirement is vacuous.

Put $r=e^{-1/4}$ and give the model prior $\pi_*=1/2$, $\pi_j=(1-r)r^{j-1}/2$. These masses sum to one. Every relative KL neighborhood has mass at least $1/2$ because it contains $*$. On any observed continuous sample, divide the prior-weighted likelihood by $\prod_i p_*(Y_i)$ to obtain the alternative numerator $A_n=e^{S_n}\sum_{j\ge1}\pi_je^{-n\epsilon_j}$. It is finite, being at most $e^{S_n}/2$, and the total relative evidence is $1/2+A_n>0$. Thus the posterior mass of the alternatives is $A_n/(1/2+A_n)$.

Almost surely, for every sufficiently large $j$, step 2.2 gives $T_j\epsilon_j\le1$ and $S_{T_j}\ge j$. Consequently $A_{T_j}\ge e^{j-1}\pi_j=(1-r)e^{j-1}r^{j-1}/2\to\infty$. Since $T_j\to\infty$, the posterior mass outside every discrete neighborhood of radius less than one has limes superior one almost surely. This contradicts the claimed a.s. consistency although both test errors in the refuted statement tend to zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC as required by the imported directional KL convention
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\rho)$ be a
metric space, where $\mathcal T$ is its Borel sigma-algebra. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sample space with a fixed sigma-finite
dominating measure. Suppose the supplied finite-valued densities
$(\theta,x)\mapsto p_\theta(x)$ and $x\mapsto p_0(x)$ are jointly measurable
and normalized relative to $\mu$, and observations are IID from $P_0$. Use
the directional convention for [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]:
$$K(\theta):=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta).$$
Assume $K^*:=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}K(\theta)<\infty$ and
$$\Theta^*:=\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta)=K^*\}\ne\varnothing.$$
The set $\Theta^*$ is the **KL projection set** of the truth onto the model.
The **distance to the KL projection set** is
$$d(\theta,\Theta^*):=\inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta^*}\rho(\theta,\vartheta).$$
A **relative KL neighborhood** of $\Theta^*$ of radius $\epsilon>0$ is
$$B_\epsilon:=\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta)-K^*\le\epsilon\}.$$

For any selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ with finite contrast, the relative
contrast on $B_\epsilon$ satisfies
$$K(\theta)-K^*=-\mathbb E_{P_0}\log\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}$$
whenever the displayed log ratio is integrable. This definition allows
$\Theta^*$ to contain multiple parameters and does not assert that the
posterior selects one of them.

Fix a selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ as in
[[def-kl-projection-set-and-relative-kl-neighborhoods]]. Since its KL value is
finite, $p_{\theta^*}>0$ $P_0$-almost surely. For each $\theta\in\Theta$,
define the nonnegative set function
$$Q_\theta(A):=\int_A\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)}\,P_0(dx), \qquad A\in\mathcal A,$$
where the ratio is assigned value $0$ on the $P_0$-null set
$\{p_{\theta^*}=0\}$. Write
$$q_\theta:=Q_\theta(\mathsf X) =\mathbb E_{P_0}\left[\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}\right]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $q_\theta\ne1$, $Q_\theta$ is not a probability law. The local
sigma-finiteness lemma proves that it is a measure. The local product-measure
lemma then constructs $Q_\theta^n$ and proves its density relative to $P_0^n$
is $\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(X_i)/p_{\theta^*}(X_i)$.

For a measurable test $\phi_n:\mathsf X^n\to[0,1]$,
Once that product measure has been constructed,
$Q_\theta^n(1-\phi_n)$ means the nonnegative integral of $1-\phi_n$ under it.
It may be infinite; a hypothesis that this quantity tends to zero in
particular requires it to be finite for all sufficiently large $n$.

Under the hypotheses and conventions of
[[def-likelihood-tilted-measure-at-kl-projection]], each $Q_\theta$ is a
sigma-finite measure. The definition does not require its total mass to be
one; the companion examples exhibit masses below and above one, while
$Q_{\theta^*}(\mathsf X)=1$ for the selected minimizer.

Under the setup of [[def-likelihood-tilted-measure-at-kl-projection]] and
[[lem-likelihood-tilted-measure-is-sigma-finite]], for each $\theta$ and
integer $n\ge1$, the sigma-finite product measure $Q_\theta^n$ exists and
has density
$$\prod_{i=1}^n r_\theta(x_i),\qquad r_\theta(x):=\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)},$$
relative to $P_0^n$. Ratios are zero where $p_{\theta^*}=0$, as in the
likelihood-tilt definition.

Let $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ be IID real random variables with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $\mathbb EX_1=0$, and $\mathbb P(X_1=0)<1$. Put $S_0=0$ and $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. Then
$$\mathbb P\left(\sup_{n\ge0}S_n=+\infty\right)=1.$$
In particular, $\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_n=+\infty$ almost surely.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.
